query: For a Hf-Mo-Ta-Ti-Zr system known to form a single-phase BCC structure with asymmetric XRD peaks due to micro-segregation (dendritic vs. interdendritic), the room-temperature fracture strain is significantly lower than theoretically expected or reported in similar systems with slight compositional variations. Propose a hypothesis where the addition of ~4 at.% of a specific transition metal (Cr) drives the formation of a complex multicomponent Laves phase with a volume fraction of approximately 4%. The hypothesis must explain how the morphology of this secondary phase (reticulated/interconnected) impedes crack extension and how the lattice distortion from the solute contributes to solid solution hardening. Define the boundary condition regarding the lattice parameter shift (contraction) and design a discriminating measurement to separate the effects of compositional micro-segregation from the added alloying element's specific phase formation.

generation.hypothesis: The addition of ~4 at.% Cr to the Hf-Mo-Ta-Ti-Zr system exceeds the solubility limit of Cr in the BCC matrix, driving the precipitation of a complex Laves phase (C14/C15) with a volume fraction of ~4% at interdendritic boundaries. This phase forms a reticulated, interconnected network that acts as a continuous brittle path for crack propagation, overriding the ductility potential of the matrix. Concurrently, the dissolution of Cr in the BCC matrix causes lattice parameter contraction due to its smaller atomic radius relative to Hf/Zr/Ti, contributing to solid solution hardening that increases yield strength but reduces strain hardening capacity, leading to premature fracture.
generation.material_initial_state: A single-phase BCC high-entropy alloy (Hf-Mo-Ta-Ti-Zr) characterized by significant micro-segregation (dendritic vs. interdendritic regions) and asymmetric XRD peaks, exhibiting low room-temperature fracture strain.
generation.intervention: Addition of approximately 4 at.% Chromium (Cr) to the alloy composition.
generation.conditions: Solidification from the melt followed by homogenization heat treatment (e.g., 1200°C for 24h) to facilitate phase separation while retaining the interdendritic network morphology.
generation.structural_mediator: A reticulated (interconnected) network of complex Laves phase (C14 or C15 structure) precipitating preferentially at the interdendritic boundaries where micro-segregation is highest.
generation.mechanism: The Laves phase forms a brittle, interconnected network that serves as a continuous path for crack propagation, bypassing crack-bridging or deflection mechanisms. Concurrently, Cr atoms dissolved in the BCC matrix cause significant lattice distortion and a net lattice parameter contraction (due to Cr's smaller atomic radius relative to Hf/Zr/Ti), leading to solid solution hardening that increases yield strength but reduces strain hardening capacity, thereby promoting early fracture.
generation.predicted_outcome: The fracture strain will remain low or decrease further compared to the Cr-free baseline, despite increased yield strength. XRD will show a distinct shift of the BCC (110) peak to higher 2θ angles (lattice contraction) and the appearance of weak Laves phase peaks. Fractography will reveal intergranular fracture along the interdendritic Laves network.
generation.baseline: The original Hf-Mo-Ta-Ti-Zr alloy without Cr, which exhibits low fracture strain attributed solely to micro-segregation-induced stress concentrations but lacks the specific brittle Laves phase network.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis holds only if the Cr concentration is sufficient to exceed the solubility limit in the BCC matrix at the solidification temperature, specifically resulting in a Laves phase volume fraction between 3% and 5%. If Cr remains fully dissolved or forms a different phase (e.g., sigma), the mechanism fails. The lattice parameter shift must be a contraction.
generation.uncertainty: There is uncertainty regarding the exact crystal structure (C14 vs C15) of the Laves phase formed in this specific quinary system, as well as the precise threshold of Cr concentration required to form a continuous reticulated network versus isolated particles. The interaction between the pre-existing micro-segregation and the new Cr-induced segregation may lead to non-uniform distribution.

falsification_experiment.design: Synthesize two batches: Batch A (Hf-Mo-Ta-Ti-Zr + 4 at.% Cr) and Batch B (Hf-Mo-Ta-Ti-Zr + 4 at.% V, a similar transition metal with different Laves-forming tendency). Process both under identical solidification and homogenization conditions (1200°C for 24h). Perform high-resolution synchrotron XRD and atom probe tomography (APT).
measurements: Lattice parameter of the BCC matrix (via Rietveld refinement of XRD)
Volume fraction and morphology of secondary phases (via SEM/EBSD and APT)
Fracture strain and yield strength (via tensile testing)
Cr concentration in the BCC matrix vs. secondary phase (via APT)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: The hypothesis is falsified if: (1) Batch A shows no Laves phase formation or the phase is isolated (not reticulated) despite 4 at.% Cr; (2) Batch A shows a lattice expansion or no shift in the BCC peak (contradicting the contraction prediction); or (3) Batch A exhibits significantly higher fracture strain than Batch B due to the absence of the brittle network, indicating the Laves phase did not form or was not detrimental.

Because modern jet engines require larger and larger parameters, improved creep properties are essential for the aerospace industry. The currently used Ni-based superalloys are reaching their limits, and since the beginning of the 21st century new alloys known as High Entropy Alloys (HEAs) have begun to look attractive [ [1] , [2] ]. HEAs can be regarded as solid solution alloys that contain at least five alloying elements in equal or near equal atomic percentages, and this large number of alloying elements results in maximizing the configurational entropy of the disordered solid solution. However, the microstructure of certain HEAs can include nano-precipitates, ordered solid-solution phases, disordered solid-solution phases, and even amorphous phases [ [1] , [2] ]. In this study, bulk samples of a CrMoNbWV high-entropy alloy (HEA) were obtained for the first time by spark plasma sintering (SPS) of mechanically alloyed (MA) powders at 1200 °C, 1300 °C, and 1400 °C. Microstructure evolution, phase formation as well as wear and corrosion behavior were investigated. The MA powders’ phase composition was found to be represented by body-centered-cubic (BCC) solid solution. The solid solution partially decomposed to Laves phases under the sintering, such as Cr 2 Nb and (Fe, Cr)Nb, and NbVO 4 -VO oxides mixture. The temperature increase to 1400 °C led to a grain coarsening of the BCC phase and decreased the Laves phase content accompanied by precipitation at the grain boundaries. The sintered samples showed high hardness and compressive strength (2700–2800 MPa) at room temperature. The wear tests demonstrated excellent results in comparison to conventional wear-resistant composites. The obtained samples also exhibited high corrosion resistance under electrochemical tests in H 2 SO 4 solution.
